title: Sun salutation, plainly
hookLine: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, then learns from it; the bow inside the yoga sequence
carry: surya namaskar is a bow to the sun
last: THE BODY AS TEMPLE — SOMEONE HOLY LIVES HERE.

lines: A HUNGRY BABY. AN ORANGE FRUIT.
cards: A baby wakes up hungry and looks out at the sky. There, low on the horizon, is a huge, glowing, orange fruit. So he jumps for it.
This is no ordinary baby. He's the son of the wind, and he flies straight up toward the rising sun, higher and higher. The gods panic.
Indra, king of the gods, hurls his thunderbolt and strikes the child on the jaw, and he falls. The jaw, hanu in Sanskrit, gives him his name: Hanuman.

teach.h: HANUMAN GRABS AT THE SUN, THEN BOWS TO IT.
teach.b: That's how the Ramayana tells it, and the story doesn't end with the fall. The wind god, his father, is so grieved that he stops blowing, and the gods have to heal the child and bless him.
In later tellings, the boy who grabbed at the sun comes back to it as a student. Surya agrees to teach him, and Hanuman learns by moving across the sky, facing his teacher from sunrise to sunset.
Grabbing at the sun, then bowing to it. Hindus honor the sun as the god you can see, and as a teacher of light.

teach.h: SURYA + NAMASKAR: A BOW TO THE SUN.
teach.b: That's the bow in surya namaskar: surya, the sun, and namaskar, a bow, from the same root as namaste, your very first word. In its common form it's a flowing loop of about twelve positions, each with a breath.
People who practice it as devotion often add what the gym leaves out: one of the sun's twelve names with each round.

teach.h: OM MITRAYA NAMAH: TO THE FRIEND.
teach.b: The first is Om Mitraya namah: a bow to Mitra, the friend. Now, plainly, the history.
Honoring the sun is very old, but this flowing sequence was made popular in the early twentieth century by a raja in western India, for health.
An old devotion in a fairly new shape. So in a yoga class it can be a stretch, and at home, facing east at dawn, it can be a bow. What makes it a salutation is who you have in mind.

how: Many Hindus practice surya namaskar in the morning, facing east, as both exercise and devotion, sometimes reciting one of the twelve names of the sun, such as Om Mitraya namah, with each round.

o: a hymn sung facing the rising sun
a dance for rain at harvest time
a bow to the sun, in movement and breath

games.q: your yoga teacher calls sun salutations 'just a warm-up.' a Hindu classmate does them facing east, saying a name of the sun each round. who's right?
o: only the teacher: it's exercise, nothing more.
it can be both: a stretch, and a bow to the sun.
only the classmate: doing it as exercise is wrong.
games.why: the name means a bow to the sun. the sequence is fairly new, the devotion old; who you have in mind makes it a salutation.

practice: Three gentle rounds, standing or sitting tall, facing east if you know where it is; skip anything that hurts, or stay seated and just move your arms.
Palms at your chest: breathe in and reach up, out and fold as far as is comfortable, in to lift halfway, out to fold, in to rise all the way up, arms high, out with palms back to the chest.
Twice more, slowly, saying the friend's name with each round if you'd like, then sit and notice whatever warmth is there.

wordCard.voice: Surya namaskar. A bow to the sun: a flowing loop of positions, one breath each, done as exercise, as devotion, or both. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sūrya, the sun, and namaskāra, a bow or salutation.

carryVoice: Your line: surya namaskar is a bow to the sun. Hanuman grabbed at the sun, then bowed to it as his teacher. Day one hundred twenty-six, done.
